title: The Qualities of Tihāīs
summary: The three uses of a tihāī: it completes a tāla cycle when an improvised passage runs short or long, brings out the note on sam, and creates an exchange with the drummer. A table gives tihāīs from three to sixteen beats in Tīntāl, followed by the arithmetic for a chakkardār tihāī spanning several cycles.

blocks.verse:
तालावर्तन पूर्तिश्च वैचित्र्यं गतगीतयोः।
संगति स्ताल वाद्येन त्रिधायीनाम् त्रयो गुणाः।१४६।
blocks.text: Completing the cycle of the tāla, bringing variety to gat and song, and companionship with the tāla instrument (drum): these are the three qualities of tihāīs.
Whatever kind a tihāī (a phrase played three times to land on sam) may be, it has three kinds of quality.

(1) When a flute player wants to present one of his rāgas with a tāla instrument (drum), he wants to show his own special brilliance by conceiving, within the gat (instrumental composition), ālāps (slow elaborations) or tāns (fast runs) of his own making. On that occasion, if the ālāp or tān comes out somewhat shorter or longer than the āvartan (cycle) of the tāla, the tihāī becomes an engaging bridge and helps the player to complete it within the tāla.
(2) By bringing out the note that stands on sam (the first beat) in the gat, it increases the beauty of the rāga.
(3) By establishing a special kind of relationship with the tāla player, it creates a fresh attraction for the listeners.

On the basis of the above rule, tihāīs from three mātrās (beats) up to sixteen mātrās are being written [below]. By counting these well, practitioners (sādhakas) will be able to make tihāīs in the same way in various rāgas and in various tālas.

Even bigger tihāīs than these can be made. If a tihāī is made of more than one āvartan (cycle) of the tāla, it is called a cakkardār (circling) tihāī. To the number of mātrās (beats) of the tihāī you want to make, add one more mātrā, divide it by 3, and make a group of notes suited to the rāga, of as many mātrās as there are in one part, with the sam note at its end, or with the sam note on the resting (virām) mātrā. By doing this, every kind of tihāī can be made. For example, two cycles of Tīntāl make 32 mātrās; adding one mātrā to them and dividing the total of 33 mātrās into three parts gives 11 mātrās per part. Now, according to rāga Bhūpālī, a series of notes of 11 mātrās was made in double tempo, keeping (Ga) at the end. (SaRe GaPa DhaṠa DhaPa GaRe SaRe PaGa -Sa -Re Ga) By playing this three times, a tihāī of 11*3 = 33 mātrās was made. In the same way tihāīs of four cycles and of five cycles can also be made. For more information on this subject, works devoted mainly to tāla can be consulted.
